candidates.attacker_control: The attacker fully controls the JWT string: the Base64url-encoded header JSON (setting "alg":"none"), the Base64url-encoded payload JSON with arbitrary claims (e.g., sub/iss/aud/custom claims and a far-future exp), and the trailing dot that marks the empty signature segment. No key material or prior valid token is required.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether the unsecured path is already rejected when verifiers exist: it is not - both guards (lines 70, 125) require the verifier collection to be empty, and the private decode's two rejection checks (lines 159, 164) do not cover the 2-part/null-verifier combination. Checked whether any Verifier implementation supports Algorithm.none (grep of canVerify): only HMACVerifier (HS256/384/512) and RSAVerifier (RS256/384/512) exist, both false for none, so verifier stays null. Checked the three-segment form with alg:none: it is rejected by MissingVerifierException (line 159), so the bypass specifically requires the trailing-dot two-segment form, which getParts permits (line 192). Checked whether exp/nbf checks mitigate: they are claim checks the attacker controls (null/omitted nbf and far-future exp pass), so they are not a mitigation. Checked the kid/Map overload: a missing or unknown kid yields a null verifier through the same path, so the flaw is shared by both overloads via the private decode. Noted that the in-repo README advertises a signature-validation fix in versions >= 1.3.0 and pom.xml declares 1.3.0, but the control flow above is present in this snapshot, so version metadata does not demonstrate the behavior is fixed; the source semantics are evaluated as-is.
candidates.impact: Signature-verification bypass / token forgery: a remote attacker who can supply a JWT to an application using this decoder as documented receives an arbitrary forged JWT (subject, issuer, audience, expiry, custom roles/claims), enabling authentication and authorization bypass. No secret or valid signed token is needed. Integrity of all claims is lost for affected decode calls.
candidates.prerequisites: The application decodes an attacker-supplied token with at least one Verifier, i.e. the repository's documented usage `JWT.getDecoder().decode(encodedJWT, verifier)` (README lines 28-34, 53-59), or the kid-based `decode(encodedJWT, verifiers)` / `decode(encodedJWT, verifiers, keyFunction)` overloads, and treats the returned JWT as authenticated. This is a library pre-condition, not an attacker pre-condition; exploitability depends on the deployment following the documented decode pattern.
candidates.root_cause: In JWTDecoder, the unsecured-token branch is guarded by `parts.length == 2 && verifiers.length == 0` (line 70) and `parts.length == 2 && verifiers.isEmpty()` (line 125). These conditions only handle the case where the caller passed no verifiers. When verifiers are supplied and the attacker-controlled header algorithm is `none`, the selection loop (lines 80-84) / lookup (lines 134-140) finds no verifier supporting `none` (Algorithm.none is accepted by no Verifier implementation; HMACVerifier only supports HS256/384/512 and RSAVerifier only RS256/384/512), leaving `verifier == null`. The private decode (lines 153-174) rejects only `parts.length == 3 && verifier == null` (MissingVerifierException, line 159) and `parts.length == 2 && verifier != null` (InvalidJWTSignatureException, line 164); the cross product `parts.length == 2 && verifier == null` is unhandled, so the `parts.length == 3` verification block (lines 168-172) is skipped and the payload segment is deserialized and returned (line 174). getParts (lines 189-196) explicitly accepts the two-segment form `XXXXX.YYYYY.` (trailing dot, empty signature), so this is a reachable, well-formed token shape.
candidates.title: JWTDecoder accepts unsigned "alg:none" tokens even when verifiers are supplied, bypassing signature verification
candidates.trace: 1) Attacker crafts `<b64url({"alg":"none"})>.<b64url(claims)>` with a trailing dot (empty signature). 2) getParts (lines 189-196) splits on '.', Java drops the trailing empty segment, `encodedJWT.endsWith(".")` is true, so a 2-element array is returned. 3) Header is deserialized (line 67/123) and `header.algorithm == Algorithm.none`. 4) The line-70 guard `parts.length == 2 && verifiers.length == 0` is false because the caller supplied a verifier; the token is not rejected here. 5) The verifier-selection loop (lines 80-84) / map lookup (lines 134-140): canVerify(Algorithm.none) is false for HMACVerifier (lines 56-65) and RSAVerifier (lines 61-70), so `verifier` remains null. 6) Private decode is invoked with `verifier == null`; check at line 159 requires parts.length == 3 (false), check at line 164 requires verifier != null (false); the verification block at lines 168-172 requires parts.length == 3 (false), so no signature is ever checked. 7) `Mapper.deserialize(base64Decode(parts[1]), JWT.class)` (line 174) returns the attacker's claims as a JWT; only attacker-adjustable exp/nbf checks run (lines 176-184). The application receives an "authenticated" JWT that was never verified.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no tests exist in the snapshot, so the bypass was not runtime-confirmed. Whether a given downstream application passes a verifier to decode (and treats the result as trusted) is assumed from the repository's documented usage examples and cannot be verified from this source tree alone. The exact rationale for the guard as written (oversight vs. intentional support for unsecured tokens with verifiers) is inferred from the adjacent comments and the MissingVerifierException/InvalidJWTSignatureException checks, which show the intent to reject unverifiable tokens.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (CWE-347) - unsigned/unsecured JWT accepted despite configured verifier

coverage_summary: Scope reported 35 model-visible files, with 0 excluded by symlink, sensitive-name/path, size, or binary filters; the same filters apply to B0 and P1. All 35 files were enumerated and, except for trivial enums/exceptions/value classes (.gitignore, JWTException and subclasses, Type, KeyType, PublicKeyUse-equivalent, RSAKeyPair, JSONWebKey, serializers), every file with executable logic was read in full, including JWTDecoder, JWTEncoder, JWT, Header, Algorithm, Signer/Verifier, HMACSigner/Verifier, RSASigner/Verifier, RSAUtils, PEMUtils, JWTUtils, OpenIDConnect, Mapper, JacksonModule, ZonedDateTime (de)serializers, and pom.xml/README.md. Searches covered canVerify implementations, Algorithm.none usage, parts.length checks, ObjectInputStream, and Runtime/ProcessBuilder. No test sources exist in the snapshot, so there are no test names or expected-behavior fixtures to corroborate or refute the finding.
limitations: Static source review only; no code was compiled or executed and no scanner/exploit was run, so the candidate is a source-evidenced lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
No test directory or test cases are included in the 35-file snapshot, so expected decode behavior could not be cross-checked against the project's own tests.

Exploitability depends on downstream application usage: an application must call JWTDecoder.decode with at least one Verifier and treat the returned JWT as authenticated; that usage is documented in the README but cannot be confirmed for real deployments from this tree.

Per the task constraints, no external patch, CVE/CWE database, or upstream repository history was consulted; the version declared in pom.xml/README could not be used to reason about whether this snapshot is pre- or post-fix, so the analysis relies solely on the source semantics present.
The intent behind the guard at line 70/125 (oversight vs. deliberate support for unsecured tokens) is inferred from surrounding comments and exceptions rather than documentation.

rejected_leads.lead: Verifier selection loop overwrites instead of stopping (JWTDecoder lines 80-84): javadoc says the first matching verifier is used, but the loop keeps assigning, so the last matching verifier wins. Could matter if a caller supplies multiple verifiers for the same algorithm.
rejected_leads.reason: Real doc/code inconsistency, but all supplied verifiers are caller-trusted by construction; no source evidence of a concrete attacker-controlled bypass distinct from the selected candidate. Left unconfirmed and not selected due to weaker security impact.

rejected_leads.lead: Non-constant-time comparison of HMAC values (HMACVerifier line 78 uses Arrays.equals) may permit a timing side channel to recover MAC bytes.
rejected_leads.reason: Theoretical and impractical to exploit over a network in this design (no attacker-controlled oracle loop demonstrated, JIT/network noise), and it does not enable the primary forgery described above. Rejected as a weaker, unverified lead.

rejected_leads.lead: Malformed PEM handling in RSAUtils/PEMUtils (e.g., getKeyBytes uses indexOf of prefix/suffix and substring; missing suffix yields StringIndexOutOfBoundsException, invalid Base64 throws IllegalArgumentException).
rejected_leads.reason: Inputs are configuration/operator-supplied key material, not remote attacker input in the normal flow; worst case is a local/config-time exception, not a security-boundary bypass. Rejected.

rejected_leads.lead: OpenIDConnect.generate_hash supports only RS256/RS384/RS512 although at_hash/c_hash are also needed for HMAC algorithms, and c_hash uses 256 left-most bits while at_hash uses 128.
rejected_leads.reason: Spec-compliance/functional limitation of a helper invoked by the token issuer, not attacker-controlled, and at_hash/c_hash values are consumed by the relying party, not this class. No concrete security impact demonstrated. Rejected.

rejected_leads.lead: ZonedDateTimeDeserializer converts attacker JSON numbers/strings to Instant.ofEpochSecond; extreme values raise DateTimeException and unknown/missing alg causes an NPE from switch on a null enum in the verifier-selection loop (JWTDecoder line 81).
rejected_leads.reason: At most denial-of-service/500-error behavior on malformed tokens, and it is secondary to the selected verification bypass. Rejected.

rejected_leads.lead: JacksonMapper is a default ObjectMapper without polymorphic typing; JWT.claims values are Object and could be abused for deserialization gadgets.
rejected_leads.reason: Checked Mapper/JacksonModule: no default typing, no activateDefaultTyping, and no target type resolves attacker-controlled class names, so no gadget path is evident. Rejected.

summary: Reviewed the 35-file prime-jwt snapshot (no files excluded by the scope filters; no test sources present). The strongest source-evidenced issue is in JWTDecoder: an unsigned token with header {"alg":"none"} and a trailing-dot empty signature is accepted and deserialized even when the caller supplies one or more Verifier instances, so signature verification is skipped entirely. The guard that is meant to restrict unsecured tokens (`parts.length == 2 && verifiers.length == 0` at line 70, and the equivalent `verifiers.isEmpty()` at line 125) only covers the zero-verifier case; with verifiers supplied, no built-in Verifier canVerify(Algorithm.none), so `verifier` remains null, and the private decode rejects neither a 2-part/no-verifier combination nor verifies anything, returning forged claims as a valid JWT. This matches the documented usage pattern in the repository README (decode(token, verifier)), making it a realistic authentication/claims-forgery bypass for consumers. Other candidate leads (last-matching-verifier selection, non-constant-time MAC compare, PEM parsing exceptions, OIDC hash helper limits) were weaker and are listed as rejected leads.
